verses.text: Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he became king, and he ruled in Jerusalem for eleven years. His mother's name was Hamutal, daughter of Jeremiah from Libnah.
He did what was evil in the LORD's sight, just as Jehoiakim had done.
It was because of the LORD's anger that all this happened to Jerusalem and Judah, until he finally removed them from his presence. Then Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon.

So on the tenth day of the tenth month of Zedekiah's ninth year as king, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon marched against Jerusalem with his whole army. They camped outside the city and built siege works all around it.
The city was kept under siege until the eleventh year of King Zedekiah.
By the ninth day of the fourth month the famine in the city was so bad that there was no food for the people.

Then the city wall was broken through, and all the soldiers ran away. They left the city at night through the gate between the two walls near the king's garden, even though the Babylonians surrounded the city. They headed toward the Jordan Valley,
but the Babylonian army chased the king and caught up with Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho. His whole army had deserted him.
They captured the king and took him to the king of Babylon at Riblah in the land of Hamath, where he passed sentence on him.
At Riblah the king of Babylon killed Zedekiah's sons while Zedekiah watched. He also killed all the officials of Judah.
Then he put out Zedekiah's eyes, bound him in bronze chains, and took him to Babylon. He kept him in prison until the day he died.
On the tenth day of the fifth month, in the nineteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, Nebuzaradan, the commander of the guard, who served the king of Babylon, came to Jerusalem.
He set fire to the LORD's temple, the king's palace, and all the houses in Jerusalem. Every important building he burned down.
The whole Babylonian army under the commander of the guard tore down all the walls around Jerusalem.

Nebuzaradan, the commander of the guard, took into exile some of the poorest people, the rest of the people left in the city, those who had deserted to the king of Babylon, and the rest of the craftsmen.
But Nebuzaradan, the commander of the guard, left behind some of the poorest people of the land to work the vineyards and fields.
The Babylonians broke up the bronze pillars, the movable stands, and the large bronze basin called the Sea that were in the LORD's temple. They carried all the bronze to Babylon.
They also took away the pots, shovels, wick trimmers, sprinkling bowls, dishes, and all the bronze objects used in the temple service.
The commander of the guard took away the basins, fire pans, sprinkling bowls, pots, lampstands, dishes, and bowls used for drink offerings, everything made of pure gold or silver.
The bronze from the two pillars, the Sea, the twelve bronze bulls under it, and the movable stands, which King Solomon had made for the LORD's temple, was too heavy to weigh.
Each pillar was twenty-seven feet tall and eighteen feet around. Each was hollow, and its metal was four fingers thick.
On top of each pillar was a bronze capital seven and a half feet high, decorated all around with a network of bronze pomegranates. The second pillar, with its pomegranates, was just like the first.
There were ninety-six pomegranates on the sides. In all, there were one hundred pomegranates above the network around the capital.
The commander of the guard took as prisoners Seraiah the chief priest, Zephaniah the priest next in rank, and the three doorkeepers.

From the city he also took the officer in charge of the soldiers, seven of the king's advisers who were found in the city, the secretary of the army commander who called up the people of the land for the army, and sixty of the people of the land who were found in the city.
Nebuzaradan, the commander of the guard, took them all and brought them to the king of Babylon at Riblah.
There at Riblah, in the land of Hamath, the king of Babylon had them executed. So the people of Judah were taken into exile, away from their land.
This is the number of people Nebuchadnezzar took into exile: in his seventh year, three thousand twenty-three Jews;
in Nebuchadnezzar's eighteenth year, eight hundred thirty-two people from Jerusalem;
in Nebuchadnezzar's twenty-third year, Nebuzaradan the commander of the guard took seven hundred forty-five Jews into exile. In all, four thousand six hundred people were taken.

In the thirty-seventh year of the exile of Jehoiachin king of Judah, on the twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month, Evil-Merodach became king of Babylon. In the first year of his reign he showed kindness to Jehoiachin king of Judah and freed him from prison.
He spoke kindly to him and gave him a seat of honor higher than the other kings who were with him in Babylon.
So Jehoiachin took off his prison clothes, and for the rest of his life he ate regularly at the king's table.
Every day the king of Babylon gave him an allowance, as long as he lived, until the day he died.
